motion: Is moral realism true: are there stance-independent moral facts or truths that survive the leading semantic, metaphysical, and epistemic objections?

burdenRoutes.description: Establish at least one stance-independent moral truth through a secure concrete judgment and defend an epistemically credible route to knowing that truth.
burdenRoutes.successCriteria: This route succeeds if the pro side establishes a true moral proposition, shows that its truth is independent of actual or hypothetical stances, and preserves a credible epistemic route to it against the debate's explanatory objections.

bridges.description: Establish that at least one stance-independent moral fact or truth exists, which is sufficient for the debated realist conclusion.
Establish the truth of a concrete moral judgment, such as the wrongness of causing enormous suffering for trivial convenience.
Show that the concrete judgment is true because of attitude-independent features rather than approval, desire, culture, or divine command.
Provide a credible epistemology on which rational reflection can disclose abstract moral truths and those truths can explain moral belief.
Compare the total plausibility of realism and error theory rather than requiring a single knockout, including the costs of each package.
Show that desire-relative instrumental reasons cannot exhaust moral or epistemic criticism because some criticism persists despite contrary desires.

burdenRoutes.description: Establish error-theoretic anti-realism by denying moral facts explanatory or evidential standing and supplying nonmoral accounts of deliberation and criticism.
burdenRoutes.successCriteria: This route succeeds if the con side shows that stance-independent moral facts lack adequate evidence or explanatory necessity and that moral intuitions, deliberation, and criticism can be explained without them.

bridges.description: Establish that there are no stance-independent moral facts or truths of the kind asserted by the realist side.
Show that nonmoral facts fully explain moral experiences and intuitions, so those experiences provide no evidence for moral facts.
Show that desire-relative instrumental relations adequately explain deliberative reasons and criticism without categorical moral reasons.
Preserve philosophical and a priori knowledge without external abstract moral facts by treating such knowledge as analytic reflection on concepts.
Require a nonaccidental connection between an experience and a claimed fact before the experience can count as evidence for that fact.

source.limitations: The source is an auto-generated English ASR caption track without embedded speaker labels. Caption windows overlap and punctuation, capitalization, and recognition errors are preserved. No local audio verification was supplied, so only moderator-signposted openings or sustained exchanges with unambiguous argumentative ownership were selected; rapid or mixed-speaker boundaries were excluded.

inventoryProtocol.selectionStatement: Selected one atomic load-bearing act from each side's first and second moderator-signposted opening constructive. The responsive phase runs from 00:31:24 to 01:41:36 and was divided into four equal 17:33 quarters: [00:31:24, 00:48:57), [00:48:57, 01:06:30), [01:06:30, 01:24:03), and [01:24:03, 01:41:36]. Two high-confidence, single-speaker responsive acts were selected chronologically from each quarter; the reviewed sample contains seven pro moves and five con moves.
